title: A Welcoming Reading Nook
subtitle: Use student observations and a class survey to plan a shared reading space
summary: The library wants a small reading nook that works for different readers. Listen to student ideas, read about welcoming shared spaces, examine a survey, and recommend a careful first setup.

briefing.scene: Your school library has one quiet corner to improve. Students read alone, with a partner, or while looking at pictures. The librarian asks your design team to use the class survey and make a plan that can be tested before more furniture is ordered.
briefing.goal: Use a student observation and survey evidence to explain a welcoming first setup, then apply your reasoning to a new shared space.

turns.speaker: Librarian Chen
turns.text: Some readers like a quiet place to read alone. Other students enjoy looking at a book with a partner. The corner is small, so people need a clear path to the shelves.

turns.speaker: Ari
turns.text: I like the picture books near the window, but sometimes the chairs block the path. I want a place where a partner can join me without moving other readers.

turns.speaker: Librarian Chen
turns.text: The class survey shows different choices. We have two floor cushions and one small rug to try this week. We can observe the corner before choosing more furniture.

report.title: Designing a shared reading space
text: A welcoming reading space gives people more than one comfortable way to read. Some readers prefer a quiet seat by themselves. Partners may want to look at the same page or talk softly about a story. A small space can support both choices when furniture is placed carefully.

A clear path helps everyone move safely to books and seats. Furniture should not block a doorway, shelf, or walking route. A rug can mark a reading area, but it should lie flat so people do not trip. Before buying more items, a team can try a small arrangement and observe how readers use it.

A survey can show what a group prefers, but a vote does not tell the whole story. The team should also watch whether readers can reach the books, share a view of a page, and move through the space. One trial is a starting point. The team can ask readers what worked and adjust the plan.

phases.instructions: Notice how the reading note and class choices can guide a first setup. Think about what the survey can and cannot tell the team.

tasks.q: Why should the team leave a clear path to the shelves?

options.text: So readers can move safely to books and seats.
So the rug can cover the shelf labels.
Because students cannot read near furniture.

tasks.explain: The text explains that a clear route helps everyone move safely through the space.

options.text: The survey had three choices, so the team should buy three chairs.
A small trial can test a flexible setup.
The rug must be placed in front of every shelf.

tasks.q: How many students chose reading with a partner?

tasks.q: What is one reason to observe readers after the first setup?

options.text: A survey shows preferences, but observation can show whether readers can move and share the space.
Observation proves that every reader will choose the same seat and use the corner in exactly the same way.
The team can skip checking the path once furniture is placed.

tasks.explain: The reading explains that a survey is only a starting point; watching the space and asking readers can show what to adjust.

phases.title: Choose a first reading-corner trial
phases.instructions: Use the visitors’ ideas and class survey. Choose a practical setup that allows the team to learn before buying more furniture.

decision.q: What should the library team try first?

options.label: Place the rug and two cushions near the window, keep a clear path to the shelves, and observe how readers use the corner.
options.consequence: This uses the items available now, supports different reading choices, and leaves room to revise the setup.

board.label: Try a flexible nook and observe readers

options.label: Fill the corner with seats and block the path so more people can sit there at once.
options.consequence: This may make movement unsafe and does not test the needs described by readers.

board.label: Crowd the corner without a clear path

frames: We can check the plan by observing ___.
guided.model: I would place the small rug near the window and put the two cushions beside it, leaving a clear path to the shelves. The survey shows that 11 students chose quiet reading alone and 9 chose reading with a partner. A small shared area could give readers a choice, but the survey does not show exactly how each person will use the corner. The team can try the arrangement this week. We should watch whether partners can share a page, readers can reach books, and everyone can move safely. Then we can ask students what worked before we add more furniture.

guided.model: Dear Librarian, I recommend placing the small rug and two cushions near the window while leaving a clear path to the shelves. The survey shows that 11 students chose quiet reading alone and 9 chose reading with a partner. A small shared area may give readers more than one way to use the corner. We should try the arrangement this week and observe whether readers can reach books, share a page, and move safely. We can also ask students what worked. The survey helps us begin, but watching the space will show us what to adjust before we buy more furniture.

frames: I would set up ___ so visitors can ___.
During the trial, we should check ___.
guided.model: I would place the example cards at one end of the art table and leave open space for drawing. The new survey shows that 12 visitors want to make a project with someone, while 8 want to draw alone. The table can support both choices if people have room to move around it. The team should try the setup during one activity. We can observe whether partners have enough space and ask solo artists whether they can focus. Then the community center can adjust the table before adding more supplies.

teacherQuestions: How can one small reading area support readers who prefer different ways to read?
What can a survey tell the team, and what might observation add?
How could the team change the nook after hearing from readers?
debrief.connections: Connect shared-space design, listening to community preferences, and using a small trial to learn. Emphasize that a survey is evidence, not a complete picture of how every reader will use the nook.
